Emmanuel's Story

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.......the amazing story of a young victim of a brutal civil war who could change the way Covid-19 patients are treated

Unique Selling Point:
An amazing multi-layered human story

Summary:
From there he walked to South Africa and became a leading pulmonologist. He has just discovered a way to prevent Covid-19 deaths.

Further information:
He was born on a clay floor in a hut in a village near Djoeba in South Sudan. When he was 14 rebels bombed the village and he tried to escape. He was caught, tortured and eventually escaped to KhartoumFrom there he walked to Eritrea. There he was caught a jailed several times, beaten and jailed. He eventually escaped to Ethiopia. In Addis he lived with street people for some time on the streets and swam through the hippo-infested Ruvuma River to get to Kenia. He eventually found an uncle in Kenia and decided to come to South Africa. He went via Kenia to Arusha and Dar es Salaam. He walked through Mozambique and Zim and crossed over into South Africa when he was 17. All through Africa he carried a small New Testament with him. He slept on the streets in Johannesburg and eventually linked up with a Catholic Church. They helped him to go back to school, and he completed matric. Then he got into Medunsa and qualified as a doctor. In 2016 he specialized in pulmonology.
Today he is one of South Africa’s leading pulmonologists and has just published absolutely ground-breaking work on Covid-patients.

He says: “I am the first person in the world to discover that most people who died of COVID-19 have died because of mucus plugs and not of lung fibrosis after I did my first bronchoscopy on 24th July 2020. There are reports of mucus plugs on the post-mortem but nobody has proven it on live patients.
Attached is my study which has been approved for publication after passing peer review. I have attached the comment of peer reviewers too.

This research will alter the way many Covid patients are treated.

The title of his article is: “Observational Study of Therapeutic Bronchoscopy in Critical Hypoxemic Ventilated Patients with Covid-19 in Mediclinic Midstream hospital Pretoria-South Africa.”

Patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia who required mechanical ventilation are divided into two:
* L-type which are easy to ventilate with oxygen because their lungs expands easily, they do not need high pressure and they respond to proning position during mechanical ventilation.
* H-type which are difficult to ventilated with oxygen because the lungs are stiff, they need high pressures and they tend to stay long in the machine and most people died because of lung fibrosis.

Since the outbreak of COVID-19 bronchoscopy was indicated only for people with bleeding or those with mucus plugs on the chest x-ray or lung mass. Patients with COVID-19 when they are put on the mechanical ventilation they normal ventilated very easily for the first 5 to 7 days, then they become difficult to ventilated and they died because you cannot put air in their lungs.
Those patients have x-ray which does not show mucus plugs or collapse of the lung lobes.

I have lost three of my patients because I could not ventilate them at all, and I decided to do bronchoscopy on my patient who we could not be ventilated despite using the maximal setting. To my surprise, I found thick mucus plugs that prevent us from ventilated the lungs. After removing the mucus plugs most of the patient survive and if they died, they die because of other problems but not because we cannot ventilate them. Four weeks after my finding the Spanish doctors also report the same finding but they did theirs on patients who are stable. My studies proof that mucus plugs are problems in COVID-19 and bronchoscopy should be used frequently in the diagnosis if the doctors struggle to ventilate them. Since then we used mucolytics on our patients and the incident of mucus plugs decrease.

Interviewees:
Dr Emmanuel Taban
Dr Taban's wife
Patient who survived because of Dr Tabans's new intervention
Fr Simon Donnelky (he rescued Emmanuel from the streets, currently in the Vatican)
Brother Peter whom he considers his guardian is in Germany

Emmanuel Taban

Script:


Dominique:
He came down on Thursday the 13th of August and he stood at the kitchen table and he said to me: “Dom, I can’t breathe, you need to take me to the doctor, I need oxygen”. So, I just left everything, picked up my keys, put him in the car and sped off.
V/O:
Frantic with worry Dominique dos Santos rushed her husband Jose to the emergency unit at the Midstream Mediclinic. He had been battling Covid-19 for a few days.
Dominique:
When we had arrived and they had taken him in, they said to me that he had less than 5 percent chance of survival.
V/O:
A lung scan indicated that Jose’s lungs were severely compromised.
Jose:
I went back to the emergency and I laid on the bed. And that is all I can remember. That is all I can remember.
V/O:
Jose lost consciousness and was taken to the Covid Intensive Care Unit. He was in critical condition.
LINK:
It was here at the Midstream Mediclinic that the dos Santos family’s path crossed with that of Dr Emmanuel Taban.
V/O:
Dr Emmanuel Taban is a pulmonologist, and lung specialists are at the forefront in the battle against Covid 19. He assessed dos Santos in the ICU and immediately phoned a despairing Dominque.
Dominique:
And he said,”Look, I am going to do a procedure on you husband. I haven’t lost a patient yet, but this is a new procedure, I am going to do it.”
V/O:
He then performed the procedure. Dominique waited anxiously at home. Early the next morning news came from the hospital. Jose was better.
Dominique:
So that day I knew that what Dr Taban had done, had brought him back to us, and I think it was within 5 days he was off the ventilator and he was able to breathe on his own.
V/O:
Dr Taban’s work with critically ill Covid patients is ground-breaking and revolutionary. But what makes his work even more remarkable is that the odds were stacked against him to even be in this position.

He was born in 1979 on a mud floor of a hut in a small village in South Sudan. His mother was a single parent.
Emmanuel:
My childhood was a happy one. We did have enough in the village, we have enough food. For me I was very happy, I grew up as a happy child.
V/O:
But it was short-lived. South Sudan was in the process of gaining independence from Sudan and in a bloody civil war hundreds of thousands were killed, and millions of people were displaced. Emmanuels’ family eventually moved to Juba, the capital city of South Sudan. When he was 14, he was arrested by the military.
Emmanuel:
Then I got put in the White House, and they thought I was a spy for the rebels.
V/O:
The White House is a notorious prison in Juba, known for all kinds of atrocities and human rights violations.
Emmanuel:
And I spent about 6 weeks in the White House and that was when I got tortured, so it was a very horrible experience.
V/O:
After his release he was sent north from Juba to Khartoum and forced to convert to Islam. He eventually escaped from a religious centre and fled over the border to Eritrea. After being imprisoned there for 6 months, he decided to attempt the near-impossible for a 16-year-old street child. He was set on walking two thousand eight hundred kilometres from Eritrea, through Ethiopia via Addis Ababa to an uncle of his in Nairobi, Kenya. Against all odds he survived the journey.
LINK:
When he finally made it to his uncle’s house in Nairobi he thought he had found a safe refuge, but he was sorely disappointed.
V/O:
His uncle refused him sanctuary and suggested that he should rather go to a UN refugee camp.
Emmanuel:
I was crying, I was angry, and that was the moment I decided that I need to find my own identity. So I juts knew I was alsone in the world and have to face the reality by myself.
V/O:
Determined to succeed in life and inspired by the words ”Manufactured in South Africa” on a Coke can, young Emmanuel headed for South Africa. His journey took him from Kenya through Tanzania into Mozambique. There he found himself alone on a deserted road.
Emmanuel:
I think that time I actually felt so free when there is nothing. To be honest, I am never afraid of animals. But I am very afraid of human beings, because animals willnever hurt you, but human beings will. And that is what I learned in South Sudan.
V/O:
In Mozambique, Emmanuel eventually got help from a Catholic group, the Comboni Missionaries. They assisted him to get to Johannesburg via Zimbabwe where they took him in, helped him to matriculate and his marks were good enough to get him admitted to Medunsa to study medicine.
LINK:
Then a chance meeting at the University’s medical library changed the course of Dr Taban’s life.
V/O:
He wanted to take out a reference book and a friendly librarian helped him. The next day he saw the same girl assisting in the ICU. He didn’t know she was a physiotherapy student who worked for extra money in the library.
Matheo:
So he saw me in the ICU, and he was confused because he thought I was a librarian and then when I saw him I said, “Where is my book? I hope you took it back in the right time.” And so we started chatting.
Emmanuel:
And from there, of course, here we are. And the rest is history.
V/O:
They were married soon after and both graduated. Today they have three lovely children. After further studies Dr Taban also qualified as a pulmonologist.
Question:
What character traits attracted you to him?
Matheo:
Well, so many actually. I think the drive. He is so driven. You know, the ambition, the passion he has for his work, the compassion with which he treats his patients.
V/O:
This became even more evident when the pandemic arrived in South Africa.
LINK:
While Dr Taban was treating an even increasing number of Covid -19 patients here in the ICU, something revolutionary occurred to him.
V/O:
He was intrigued as to why some Covid patients who initially responded well to ventilation, deteriorated after a few days and then died.

He decided to do a bronchoscopy to find out what was going on in the lungs, although the World Health Organization had advised against this for Covid patients. During a bronchoscopy a thin, lighted tube is inserted into the lungs to inspect the airways. To his surprise, Dr Taban found several mucus plugs.

Inside the lungs mucus can build up and can become thick and hardened. It then acts like a plug, blocking airways and rendering ventilators ineffective. Dr Taban decided to remove the plugs he saw.
Emmanuel:
And we sucked them out , it was difficult. It took about 2 hours and a half. We sucked them out and the oxygen levels went back to normal. And we were able to take the patient out of life support after two days. So I thought that was incidental. I did a second one, the third one was exactly the same thing.
V/O:
Dr Taban was the first in the world to try this lifesaving treatment on Covid patients and has just published an academic study on his findings.

When we visited him at his rooms, we noticed several trophies on his desk. They were all from grateful patients whom he had given a second chance through his use of the therapeutic bronchoscopy technique.
UPSOUND

And among the many who are grateful that the boy from South Sudan had survived a near impossible journey through Africa, are Jose and Dominique dos Santos.
Dominique:
To me it was a miracle…
Jose:
Oh yes, definitely, the new procedure, the new intervention, did save my life.
